title: Smeltertown Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Smeltertown wells have a 100 ft median depth, 13 gpm median yield, and typical finished costs of $12,500-$22,000.
h1: Smeltertown, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Smeltertown sits in mountain bedrock near Salida and Poncha Springs, where most permitted wells draw from unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers. The local records show a 100-foot median well depth and a 13.0 gpm median reported yield, but a permit record is not a guarantee for a particular lot.

Before buying or building, compare nearby well permits, confirm the intended use with Colorado DWR, and have a driller evaluate access, geology, casing, grout, pump sizing, and the proposed septic area. The surrounding mine and environmental history also makes site-specific water testing important.

sections.heading: How deep are wells around Smeltertown?
sections.html:
Permitted wells within the Smeltertown search area have a median reported depth of 100 feet. The middle half runs from 55 to 174 feet, so many drilling bids should be based on a relatively shallow hole, while still allowing for local variation. The 90th percentile is 283 feet, and the deepest record reaches 790 feet.

The depth mix is nearly split: 46% are under 100 feet, and 45% fall from 100 to 300 feet. Only 9% are between 300 and 600 feet. Most permits identify unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, so granite and gneiss fractures, rather than a uniform sand-and-gravel layer, can control the final depth.

sections.heading: What water yield can a Smeltertown well provide?
sections.html:
Reported well yield has a median of 13.0 gpm, with the middle half from 10.0 to 15.0 gpm. That is a useful production range for typical household planning, but the yield on a permit is a tested result from a specific well, not a promise for an unbuilt well. Only 1,323 wells in the records report a pump yield, so the dataset is not complete.

61% of reported wells produce from 5 to 15 gpm, while 35% report more than 15 gpm. Another 4% fall between 1 and 5 gpm, and none are recorded under 1 gpm. A driller should still discuss storage, pump recovery, household demand, and the possibility of a fractured-rock well performing differently from its neighbors.

sections.heading: What does the water table show near Smeltertown?
sections.html:
The median static water level is 46 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 28 to 80 feet. For excavation and pump planning, that means water levels can be relatively close to the surface, but the spread matters when setting casing, locating a pump, and planning trenches.

The decade medians do not show a simple steady decline. Measurements were 72 feet below surface in the 1990s, 40 feet in the 2000s, 51 feet in the 2010s, and 43 feet in the 2020s. These are measurements from different wells and dates, so they should not be treated as a continuous monitoring record. A buyer should obtain the actual static level and pumping information for the closest comparable wells.

sections.heading: Who has drilled wells here, and how active is the record?
sections.html:
Colorado DWR records show a long drilling history around Smeltertown. The most active names are American Drilling Service (Dewberry, Bradford W.) with 805 records, Mccoy Drilling Inc (Dennison, Lynn A.) with 346, and M & M Backhoe Service (Myers, Dale T.) with 262. Those names show who appears often in the permit data; they are not a recommendation or proof of current availability.

Permits were issued across every decade shown, with the largest volume in the 2000s at 645, followed by the 1990s at 590. The newest permit year is 2026. Of 3,059 total records, 2,091 are recorded as constructed, so verify construction status before relying on any individual map point.

sections.heading: What does it cost to drill a well in Smeltertown?
sections.html:
Local cost planning should account for fractured mountain bedrock, described in the drilling model as granite and gneiss. The typical drilling rate is $65-$100 per foot. At the local median depth of 100 feet, the drilled hole works out to about $6,500-$10,000.

A finished well is more than the hole. The local model puts a completed installation, including pump, tank, trenching, and electrical, at about $12,500-$22,000. A bid can change with access, casing and grout requirements, pump capacity, trench length, power work, and whether the well reaches water at the planned depth. Ask for the assumed depth, included equipment, testing, and the handling of a dry or low-yield hole in writing.

sections.heading: Risks to check before buying a Smeltertown lot
sections.html:
Smeltertown has a substantial historic industrial and mining setting. The mapped area contains 12 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 630 historic mine features, and 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These mapped locations do not establish contamination on a particular parcel, but they are a reason to order a professional water test and review site history before closing.

Most permits name fractured bedrock, where nearby wells can differ because water follows separate fractures. Check for low-yield or abandoned wells, dry-hole records, well construction, casing, grout, and actual pumping data. Domestic or household use accounts for 84% of the use mix, while stock, irrigation, and monitoring account for 6%, 2%, and 4%. Confirm the permit allows your intended use, and keep the well and septic system separated as required by site design and regulation.

sections.heading: A practical plan for building near Smeltertown
sections.html:
Start with the closest permitted wells, not a countywide average. Compare their depths, reported yields, static levels, aquifer descriptions, construction details, and intended uses. The nearby records around Salida and Poncha Springs can provide context, but a parcel near a mapped mine feature or environmental site still needs its own review.

For a new home, have a Colorado-licensed driller inspect rig access and estimate the likely depth range before you finalize a budget. Confirm the DWR permit path, household-use limits, pump and storage design, electrical route, and septic layout together. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be required for some uses. Do not treat the median 100-foot depth or 13.0 gpm yield as a guarantee; make the purchase contingent on due diligence when the water supply is central to the property.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Smeltertown, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Smeltertown is 100 feet. The middle half of wells ranges from 55 to 174 feet, while the 90th percentile is 283 feet. Nearly half are under 100 feet, and another 45% are between 100 and 300 feet. Fractured granite and gneiss can make an individual well shallower or deeper than nearby records.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Smeltertown?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $65-$100 per foot in fractured mountain bedrock. At the 100-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $6,500-$10,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $12,500-$22,000. Access, casing, grout, pump size, trench length, and final depth can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water does a well make in Smeltertown?
faq.a: Reported wells have a 13.0 gpm median yield, with the middle half between 10.0 and 15.0 gpm. About 61% produce from 5 to 15 gpm, and 35% report more than 15 gpm. These figures come from tested permit records, not guarantees. Fractured-bedrock wells can vary sharply, so review the closest pumping results.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Smeltertown?
faq.a: Permit records do not prove drinking-water safety. The area has 12 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 630 historic mine features, and 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those facts justify professional testing for the actual property, plus a review of nearby mine and land-use history before using the well for household water.

faq.q: Does Smeltertown have a dropping water table?
faq.a: The available decade medians do not show a steady drop. Static levels were 72 feet below surface in the 1990s, 40 feet in the 2000s, 51 feet in the 2010s, and 43 feet in the 2020s. These measurements come from different wells, so they are not a continuous trend for one aquifer. Check the closest well data for a property-specific answer.
